newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: New challenges face Philippines after IMF exit.
newsitem.headline: New challenges face Philippines after IMF exit.

text.p: The Philippines faces a fresh set of economic challenges as International Monetary Fund guidance draws to a close, a senior IMF official said on Thursday.
These include containing the trade deficit, reviving the farm sector and accelerating poverty alleviation, IMF Asia-Pacific Assistant Director John Hicklin said.
"These are the challenges the Philippines now faces. Those are the challenges of a successful emerging market," he told a news conference.
After 34 years, IMF involvement in the Philippines is scheduled to end in June.

The IMF conducted its last review of the Philippines in conjunction with a three-year Extended Fund Facility programme and a finalised memorandum is expected to be circulated to the IMF executive board at the beginning of March.
The Philippines hopes to graduate in late June under this programme, its 22nd, after 34 years of IMF involvement.
Manila officials say ending links with the IMF would firmly establish the country's credentials as a "Tiger" economy and signal to the world that the Philippines was credit-worthy.
The Extended Fund Facility programme had set out a series of reforms and economic targets to wean the Philippines away from its dependence on foreign assistance.
"I think certainly a passing mark... with honors," Hicklin said when asked about how the Philippines had rated so far with its economic performance.
He said he was optimistic the Philippines would graduate this June from the IMF despite some pending reforms.

"We are very confident of the commitment of the authorities to complete the structural reform programme...on time," Hicklin said, referring to the restructuring of corporate and income taxes, which are critical for providing a solid revenue base for the government.

The government had promised to pass this programme into law by May 1. The remaining portion of the tax reform programme had been delayed by wrangling over excise taxes on beer and cigarettes, which was finally passed in November last year.
IMF and government economic officials also announced on Thursday a series of economic targets for 1997 under the three-year Extended Fund Facility programme.
Gross national product growth had been set at seven to eight percent this year against 6.8 percent last year, they said.
Gross domestic growth was seen at just over 6.0 percent compared with 5.5 percent in 1996, officials said.

The monetary programme had set higher growth rates compared with their actual increase in 1996 even as inflation was expected to be about six to seven percent this year from 8.4 percent in 1996, Central Bank officials said.
M3, the broadest measure of liquidity, would be allowed to grow by an average 21.5 percent in 1997 versus 19.8 percent in 1996. M3 was estimated at 881.4 billion pesos at the end of 1996.
Base money, which was at estimated at 244.1 billion at the end of 1996, would have an average growth of 16.2 percent this year from the actual 13.2 percent in 1996.
Monetary management would continue to be flexible since it would take into account unexpected surges in capital inflows, officials said.
"We are confident we will meet the programme," Central Bank Governor Gabriel Singson said.
